original_title: Wire Services Stripped of Permanent White House Pool Slots

existing.title: Wire Services Stripped of Permanent White House Pool Slots
existing.description_short: Wire Services Stripped of Permanent White House Pool Slots
existing.description_long: On April 15, 2025 — one day after a court ordered AP's access restored — the White House announced it was eliminating the permanent press pool slot for wire services, ending decades of guaranteed rotation for AP, Reuters, and Bloomberg News. Under the new policy, wire services would compete for one rotating spot among approximately 30 print and newspaper outlets, effectively diluting their access to the president. Reuters, AP, and Bloomberg had collectively reached billions of people worldwide through their pool-based presidential coverage. The WHCA condemned the change as continued retaliation for independent editorial decisions. AP immediately filed in federal court, arguing the new policy was a deliberate attempt to circumvent Judge McFadden's April 8 injunction restoring its access. On May 12, 2025, all three wire services were excluded from the press pool accompanying Trump on Air Force One to Saudi Arabia, Qatar, and the UAE — the first time major international wire services had been barred from a U.S. presidential foreign trip in modern history. The White House separately suppressed at least two pool reports in early April by declining to distribute them through official channels, including one noting AP journalists had been turned away from a presidential dinner.

original_title: Trump Fires DOJ Prosecutor to Pursue Retaliatory Case Against Comey

existing.title: Trump Fires DOJ Prosecutor to Pursue Retaliatory Case Against Comey
existing.description_short: Trump Fires DOJ Prosecutor to Pursue Retaliatory Case Against Comey
existing.description_long: In September 2025, Trump orchestrated the removal of U.S. Attorney Erik Siebert from the Eastern District of Virginia after Siebert, following a five-month investigation, concluded there was not sufficient evidence to charge former FBI Director James Comey. Trump publicly pressured Siebert to resign in an Oval Office address, then fired him when he refused to quit. Trump appointed Lindsey Halligan — a former personal attorney with no prosecutorial experience — as his replacement. Halligan was sworn in on September 22, 2025, and three days later secured a federal grand jury indictment against Comey on charges of making a false statement to Congress and obstructing a congressional proceeding related to 2020 testimony — just before the five-year statute of limitations expired on September 30. Halligan accomplished the indictment despite the full grand jury never reviewing the final indictment text; only the foreperson and one other juror saw it. Federal judges described the investigation as showing a disturbing pattern of profound investigative missteps and potential prosecutorial misconduct. On November 24, 2025, Judge Cameron Currie dismissed the indictment, ruling Halligan had been unlawfully appointed. The DOJ appealed. Comey had famously been fired by Trump during his first term while overseeing the Russia investigation.

original_title: GAO Finds DOGE $215B Savings Claims Fabricated; 96% of Grants Unverifiable

existing.title: GAO Finds DOGE $215B Savings Claims Fabricated; 96% of Grants Unverifiable
existing.description_short: GAO Finds DOGE $215B Savings Claims Fabricated; 96% of Grants Unverifiable
existing.description_long: On August 6, 2026, the Government Accountability Office released a comprehensive audit of DOGE's Wall of Receipts savings claims. Of 13,476 contracts DOGE claimed to have terminated, no termination action was actually taken on 2,503 of them. In one case, DOGE continued claiming $1.7 billion in savings from a Defense Health Agency IT contract even after Pentagon officials got DOGE to agree the contract should remain — and no action was taken. DOGE had claimed $113 million in lease savings, but GAO found the actual figure was $53.5 million; 108 of 264 leases claimed as DOGE cuts were already in the termination process before DOGE existed, representing $15.3 million in misappropriated credit. For grant savings, DOGE claimed $49.2 billion but GAO could not verify 96.2 percent of it — approximately $47.32 billion — because DOGE provided no methodology or supporting data. For contract savings where methodology could be evaluated, DOGE followed its own stated approach only 27.5 percent of the time, deviated in 60.7 percent of cases, and data was missing for the rest. DOGE had originally promised $2 trillion in cuts; even its own inflated claims reached only $215 billion. DOGE refused all GAO requests for interviews, clarifications, or documentation.

existing.description_short: White House Replaces Independent Press Pool with MAGA Influencer Briefings — Conspiracy Theorists Given Oval Office Access
existing.description_long: Starting in late February 2025, the Trump White House stripped the independent White House Correspondents' Association of its century-old role in selecting the presidential press pool and replaced it with administration-controlled access, simultaneously launching weekly influencer briefings that gave White House podium time to Trump-aligned podcasters, conspiracy theorists, and former administration officials in place of credentialed journalists. Of 25 influencers identified by NBC News who attended the May 2025 briefings, all but one had a history of explicit Trump support; attendees included Jack Posobiec — who had promoted the debunked Pizzagate conspiracy theory — Dom Lucre, briefly banned from X for sharing child sexual abuse material, and 18-year-old Bo Loudon, who called himself Barron Trump's best friend. Press secretary Karoline Leavitt held separate influencer briefings running concurrently with traditional press briefings, framing the arrangement as democratizing access while simultaneously restricting traditional outlets: Reuters and Bloomberg saw access reduced, the AP was banned, and streaming outlets favorable to Trump were rotated into pool slots vacated by wire services. The Axios analysis found that MAGA-friendly journalists dilute scrutiny, denigrate Democrats and ultimately flatter President Trump. The restructuring formalized what critics called the most extensive peacetime manipulation of presidential press access in American history.

existing.title: Hegseth Forces Pentagon Press Corps Exodus: 30+ Outlets Surrender Credentials Rather Than Sign Censorship Pledge
existing.description_short: Hegseth Forces Pentagon Press Corps Exodus: 30+ Outlets Surrender Credentials Rather Than Sign Censorship Pledge
existing.description_long: Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth — a former Fox News host — issued a 17-page Pentagon press access directive in September 2025 requiring credentialed journalists to sign a pledge agreeing not to report information not approved for public release by an appropriate authorizing official, explicitly including unclassified information, under threat of credential revocation and loss of access. At least 30 major news organizations — including Reuters, AP, The New York Times, The Washington Post, Wall Street Journal, CNN, Fox News, NBC, ABC, CBS, NPR, Axios, Politico, The Guardian, The Atlantic, Bloomberg, and dozens of military-focused publications — refused to sign the policy. On October 15, 2025, the deadline day, dozens of journalists carried boxes of files, chairs, a copying machine, and personal items out of the Pentagon building in a historic departure, with roughly 40-50 reporters vacating their long-established press workspaces. The Pentagon Press Association called the new rules a direct attack on the freedom of the press. Hegseth had earlier in May 2025 required journalists to have official escorts throughout most of the Pentagon building, and had launched an aggressive internal leak investigation that resulted in the removal of senior military officials. Only One America News agreed to the new access terms.

original_title: Executive Orders Dismantle Federal DEI Programs Overnight

existing.title: Executive Orders Dismantle Federal DEI Programs Overnight
existing.description_short: Executive Orders Dismantle Federal DEI Programs Overnight
existing.description_long: On January 20 and 21, 2025, Trump signed two executive orders — EO 14151 Ending Radical and Wasteful Government DEI Programs and Preferencing and EO 14173 Ending Illegal Discrimination and Restoring Merit-Based Opportunity — that collectively dismantled decades of federal diversity infrastructure. EO 14151 required all federal agencies to terminate DEI and DEIA offices, positions, equity action plans, equity-related grants, and DEI performance requirements within 60 days. All Chief Diversity Officer positions were eliminated. On January 24, the Office of Personnel Management placed thousands of DEIA employees on paid administrative leave and ordered the removal of all DEIA-related content from agency websites. EO 14173 went further, revoking landmark civil rights executive orders dating back to Lyndon Johnson's era, including EO 11246 (Equal Employment Opportunity for federal contractors), EO 13583 (diversity in the federal workforce), and EO 13672 (non-discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity for federal contractors). This effectively stripped LGBTQ+ federal contractor employees of protections that had been in place since 2014. The orders also directed agencies to investigate private-sector DEI programs deemed illegal, designating up to nine companies for civil compliance investigations. The American Federation of Government Employees estimated over 1,000 federal employees lost their positions in DEIA offices within weeks.

original_title: Trump Federalizes California National Guard Over Governor's Objection for Immigration

existing.title: Trump Federalizes California National Guard Over Governor's Objection for Immigration
existing.description_short: Trump Federalizes California National Guard Over Governor's Objection for Immigration
existing.description_long: On June 7, 2025, President Trump issued a presidential memorandum federalizing at least 2,000 California National Guard troops over the explicit objection of Governor Gavin Newsom, invoking 10 U.S.C. §12406 — a statute that had not been used since 1970, when President Nixon federalized the Guard to deliver mail during a postal strike. The last time the Guard was federalized over a governor's objection was 1965, when President Johnson deployed it to protect civil rights marchers in Selma, Alabama. Trump's justification was that protests against ICE raids constituted rebellion against the authority of the Government of the United States. Within two days, Trump doubled the deployment to 4,000 troops and sent 700 active-duty Marines into Los Angeles — the first domestic Marine deployment in over 30 years. The memorandum described immigration protesters as insurrectionists. Governor Newsom called the deployment purposefully inflammatory. Legal scholars noted the federalized troops were subject to Posse Comitatus and could not legally conduct raids, make arrests, or detain persons — raising the concern that the administration was escalating deliberately to justify invoking the Insurrection Act. The administration had already established National Defense Areas covering one-third of the US-Mexico border, empowering soldiers to detain migrants by treating border land as Army installations.

original_title: EO Bans Transgender People from Military Service

existing.title: EO Bans Transgender People from Military Service
existing.description_short: EO Bans Transgender People from Military Service
existing.description_long: On January 27, 2025, Trump signed Prioritizing Military Excellence and Readiness, reinstating and expanding his first-term transgender military ban. The order declared that expressing a gender identity different from one's birth sex conflicts with a soldier's commitment to an honorable, truthful, and disciplined lifestyle and is inconsistent with the humility and selflessness required of a service member. It revoked Biden's EO 14004 that had allowed transgender people to serve openly and receive Tricare coverage for gender-affirming care. The new order gave the Defense Department 60 days to update medical standards, directed an immediate end to invented pronoun usage, and prohibited transgender service members from using facilities matching their gender identity. An estimated 4,240 transgender service members were affected, including decorated veterans of Iraq and Afghanistan. The order did not immediately discharge anyone but set in motion a process that would ultimately force thousands out. A federal judge initially blocked the order as unconstitutional, but on May 6, 2025, the Supreme Court's 6-3 conservative majority allowed it to take effect while litigation continued, enabling the Pentagon to begin the mass separation process. New Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth had vocally championed the ban as part of his broader campaign to rid the military of what he termed woke policies.

existing.title: Trump Pardons ~1,500 Jan 6 Defendants Including Violent Rioters
existing.description_short: Trump Pardons ~1,500 Jan 6 Defendants Including Violent Rioters
existing.description_long: On January 20, 2025, his first day back in office, Trump signed a proclamation granting blanket clemency to all approximately 1,500 people charged or convicted for their roles in the January 6, 2021 Capitol attack. The vast majority received full, complete and unconditional pardons, while 14 leaders of the Oath Keepers and Proud Boys had their sentences commuted to time served. Among those fully pardoned were over 300 people who had pleaded guilty to assaulting or obstructing law enforcement, including 69 who admitted assaulting police with a deadly weapon. Enrique Tarrio, sentenced to 22 years for seditious conspiracy, walked free. Stewart Rhodes, the Oath Keepers founder sentenced to 18 years, was released from prison the next morning. Trump referred to the convicted rioters as hostages and patriots, framing the largest federal prosecution in DOJ history as a political witch hunt. Judges who had presided over trials expressed outrage. NPR identified dozens of pardoned defendants who had prior convictions for rape, manslaughter, domestic violence, and child pornography. The order also directed the Attorney General to dismiss all pending indictments related to January 6, instantly terminating approximately 450 open cases and erasing the work of hundreds of prosecutors and law enforcement officers who had built the cases over four years.

original_title: Sam Bankman-Fried Mounts Pardon Campaign Citing Trump Crypto Fealty

existing.title: Sam Bankman-Fried Mounts Pardon Campaign Citing Trump Crypto Fealty
existing.description_short: Sam Bankman-Fried Mounts Pardon Campaign Citing Trump Crypto Fealty
existing.description_long: Beginning in January 2025 and escalating through 2025, disgraced FTX founder Sam Bankman-Fried — serving a 25-year sentence for fraud, money laundering, and conspiracy related to the $30 billion collapse of his crypto exchange — launched a high-profile campaign to obtain a presidential pardon from Trump. Bankman-Fried's parents, Stanford Law professors Joe Bankman and Barbara Fried, met with lawyers in Trump's orbit and co-wrote an op-ed praising Trump's sovereign wealth fund plans. SBF conducted an unauthorized jailhouse interview with Tucker Carlson in March 2025, which landed him in solitary confinement, positioning himself as a victim of Democratic prosecutors in the Southern District of New York. In November 2025, CNN reported that SBF was making a play for redemption with appeal arguments. Observers noted Trump's incentive structure: the SDNY prosecutors who convicted SBF were the same figures Trump had attacked in other contexts; and judge Lewis Kaplan, who oversaw SBF's trial, was the same judge who handled E. Jean Carroll's defamation case against Trump. One crypto lobbyist told Fortune that SBF's pardon odds were increasing because of Trump's increasing ties to the industry and his willingness to use his pardoning power freely. The campaign illustrated how Trump's blanket alignment with the crypto industry transformed presidential clemency into a transactional commodity.

existing.description_long: In March 2025, when senior UAE officials met Trump, the UAE committed to a 10-year, $1.4 trillion investment framework in U.S. sectors including energy, AI, and manufacturing — a commitment made while the Trump Organization was simultaneously developing new real estate projects in the Middle East and Trump family members were seeking regional business partnerships. During Trump's May 15-16, 2025 Gulf tour stop in Abu Dhabi, he announced a US-UAE AI Acceleration Partnership, unlocking the sale of advanced Nvidia AI semiconductors to the UAE for data center construction — a national security concession that previous administrations had refused on grounds of technology proliferation risk. Trump announced over $200 billion in deals during the UAE visit alone, including a $14.5 billion Etihad Airways commitment to Boeing aircraft and a framework allowing the UAE to build AI data centers matching U.S. capacity — effectively transferring critical AI infrastructure leverage to a Gulf monarchy. Al Jazeera's correspondent reported the UAE had decided to change their mind under Trump, particularly when the UAE said that it was willing to invest $1.4 trillion — making explicit that the investment pledge was the price of technology access that prior administrations had withheld on security grounds, intertwined with the Trump family's own expanding Gulf business footprint.

original_title: Gender-Affirming Care Ban - 'Chemical and Surgical Mutilation' Executive Order

existing.title: Gender-Affirming Care Ban - 'Chemical and Surgical Mutilation' Executive Order
existing.description_short: Gender-Affirming Care Ban - 'Chemical and Surgical Mutilation' Executive Order
existing.description_long: Donald Trump signed an executive order banning federal funding for gender-affirming care for people under 19, calling transgender healthcare 'chemical and surgical mutilation of children' while directing agencies to end medical treatment that doctors and families view as lifesaving for transgender youth. The January 20 order titled 'Protecting Children from Chemical and Surgical Mutilation' directed executive agencies to ensure medical institutions receiving federal grants 'end the chemical and surgical mutilation of children' through puberty blockers, hormone therapy, and surgical procedures. Trump's order instructed the Defense Secretary to exclude gender-affirming care from TRICARE military health coverage and federal employee health benefit programs, while directing HHS to withdraw March 2022 guidance supporting transgender youth healthcare. The ban aligned with Project 2025's criticism of gender-affirming care as causing 'irreversible physical and mental harm' despite medical organizations and transgender families disputing this characterization and filing lawsuits claiming the order was discriminatory. Two federal district courts blocked Trump's directive after families and doctors argued the ban would harm transgender youth who rely on medical care supported by major medical associations, with appeals pending in higher courts. The systematic targeting of transgender healthcare represented what critics called the administration's broader 'culture war' agenda that prioritized political ideology over medical expertise and family decision-making in healthcare choices.

The February 10, 2025 order instructed Attorney General Pam Bondi to 'promulgate guidelines on FCPA enforcement' while halting initiation of new investigations into foreign bribery and corruption by American companies and individuals. The FCPA freeze came alongside Bondi's issuance of 'more than a dozen policy memoranda' that 'fundamentally realigned DOJ's operations and enforcement priorities' to de-emphasize corporate investigations and prioritize other targets. Legal experts noted the freeze had 'potential to bring about a seismic shift in DOJ's approach to corporate investigations and enforcement' by providing a 180-day window for companies to avoid consequences for foreign corruption while the administration restructured enforcement priorities. The order represented a dramatic departure from decades of bipartisan FCPA enforcement that had made American companies among the world's most scrutinized for international corruption, potentially signaling to foreign partners that bribery and corruption would face reduced consequences under Trump's administration. The FCPA freeze aligned with Trump's broader pattern of protecting corporate interests and wealthy allies from federal prosecution while redirecting law enforcement resources toward political opponents and immigration targets.

original_title: Trump Administration Guts FOIA Infrastructure: DOGE Fires Records Officers, OPM Responds to CNN Request With Good Luck With That

existing.title: Trump Administration Guts FOIA Infrastructure: DOGE Fires Records Officers, OPM Responds to CNN Request With Good Luck With That
existing.description_short: Trump Administration Guts FOIA Infrastructure: DOGE Fires Records Officers, OPM Responds to CNN Request With Good Luck With That
existing.description_long: In early 2025, DOGE's mass federal workforce reductions systematically eliminated the staff responsible for processing Freedom of Information Act requests at multiple agencies, with the Office of Personnel Management responding to a CNN FOIA request for records about Elon Musk and DOGE's security clearances with the message Good luck with that — meaning the FOIA officers had been fired. Freedom of the Press Foundation's Lauren Harper warned that agencies remained legally obligated to respond within 20 business days regardless of staffing, but that courts would find it difficult to enforce compliance without personnel in place. The Trump administration also claimed that DOGE's records were covered by the Presidential Records Act and exempt from FOIA until five years after Trump left office, arguing DOGE was a presidential advisory board rather than a federal agency — a position rejected by U.S. District Judge Christopher Cooper in March 2025, though the Supreme Court blocked enforcement in June 2025. The firing of the National Archives and Records Administration head and forced resignations of senior leadership raised further alarms about preservation of government records. American Oversight and other watchdog groups filed numerous FOIA lawsuits and found systematic non-response across multiple executive agencies, documenting what Harper called an effective dismantling of the public's access to government information.

original_title: Trump Ends Sensitive Areas Protections for Churches, Schools, Hospitals

existing.title: Trump Ends Sensitive Areas Protections for Churches, Schools, Hospitals
existing.description_short: Trump Ends Sensitive Areas Protections for Churches, Schools, Hospitals
existing.description_long: On January 21, 2025, his second full day in office, President Trump signed a directive through the Department of Homeland Security revoking a 2011 Obama-era policy that designated churches, schools, hospitals, funerals, weddings, and public demonstrations as sensitive areas where ICE and CBP could not conduct immigration enforcement. The Biden administration had maintained and expanded these protections. DHS Secretary Kristi Noem framed the rollback as necessary to prevent criminals from hiding in protected spaces. Border czar Tom Homan told CNN that collateral arrests in sanctuary cities would increase as agents pursued targets in the community. Faith leaders across the country condemned the move immediately: the Episcopal Diocese of New York's Bishop Matthew Heyd noted he knew of no cases where churches had been exploited by criminals. Research showed undocumented immigrants commit crimes at lower rates than US citizens. The practical effect was profound: immigrant families began skipping medical appointments, pulling children from school, and stopping attendance at worship services out of fear. A Texas Rio Grande Valley report from July 2025 described immigrants refusing to leave their homes even for critical medication, with prediabetic women skipping pharmacy trips after seeing agents in parking lots. Legal experts warned the change would drive vulnerable people underground, undermining public health, education enrollment, and community safety.

The systematic targeting included Colombian nationals, creating diplomatic tensions when foreign governments pushed back against deportation flights.
